# New tariffs on Canadian goods could mean higher prices, new pressure on Georgia businesses

Brian  Unger

September 1, 2026 / 8:19 AM EDT
/ CBS Atlanta

As new U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods take effect and Canada is expected to respond with tariffs of its own, Georgia businesses and consumers could be particularly exposed to the economic fallout. [...] Canada is Georgia's largest international export market, and a new report from the Georgia Chamber Foundation says more than $13 billion in trade moves annually between Georgia and Canada.

The latest tariff fight comes as businesses are already confronting higher costs — some of which ultimately make their way to consumers. [...] "Since we have to buy it from somewhere else, you do kind of need to be aware of that," McClure said. "There's probably going to be a bit of an upcharge."

"In a business where the margins are pennies, we're having to spend more dollars for those same pennies," he added.

# Canada 100% Surtax on Chinese EVs

Fearing that Canada would become a dumping ground for Chinese goods blocked by US tariffs, Ottawa enacted an identical trade wall. Under Section 53 of the Customs Tariff Act, Canada applied a 100% surtax on all Chinese EVs and a 25% surtax on Chinese steel and aluminum.

100% EV Surtax 25% Aluminum Surtax

Source: Department of Finance Canada. Last verified 2026-08-27.

EVs / Hybrids

Effective Oct 2024 [...] After the Biden administration announced 100% tariffs on Chinese EVs, Canadian officials realized that millions of cheap Chinese cars would instantly pivot and flood the Canadian market, destroying domestic auto manufacturing in Ontario.

### The Tesla Loophole Closed

Prior to the tariff, Tesla was importing the Model 3 and Model Y into Canada from its Shanghai gigafactory to maximize margins. The 100% surtax forced Tesla to rapidly switch its Canadian supply chain back to its US factories.

results.title: Trump automotive tariffs, what's at risk for the EV industry?
results.content:
While some vehicles manufactured in Canada and Mexico meet USMCA requirements, many do not, largely due to the globally integrated nature of EV supply chains. As a result, a significant number of vehicles originating from these countries will still be subject to tariffs, albeit at slightly lower rates compared to other countries.

#### Europe will feel biggest impact of automotive tariffs [...] In 2024, just over 1.5 million EVs were sold in the US market. Of these, 595,000 EVs were imported equating to 38% of all US EV sales in 2024 according to Benchmark’s EV Production Quarterly Outlook. These vehicles originated from 14 countries, with Mexico accounting for the highest number followed by Japan and South Korea.

#### Canada and Mexico will feel the tariffs, but have some leniency [...] In 2024, the US produced just over 1.1 million EVs, while the majority of these went to the domestic market, just under 186,000 EVs, 17%, were exported and sold outside of the country. Most of these vehicles, 57%, remained within North America going to the US’ neighbours Canada and Mexico. Outside of the region, US-made EVs had a limited market share. The next biggest destination was Europe which sold just over 60,000 US made EVs in 2024.

results.title: TD Economics - Canadians Need to Think Strategically on Electric Vehicles and China
results.content: Canada’s tariff on Chinese EVs was implemented 4 days after the U.S. tariff went into effect, with both nations citing the risks posed to the North American market by unfair competition. This was not surprising as the two markets are heavily integrated in both production and sales. Roughly 95% of Canadian motor vehicle and parts exports are sent to the U.S. every year, while roughly 40% of U.S. motor vehicle and parts exports are sent to Canada. The former of these two statistics is largely why [...] To some degree, the challenges related to domestic prices and the charging infrastructure reflects a strategic choice the government made to confront perceptions of “dumping” into the Canadian market from China’s EV overcapacity, which was a byproduct of nearly two decades of significant subsidization of their industry to the tune of about US$230 billion1. This risked displacing domestic production through an unfair advantage, resulting in a 100% tariff on Chinese EVs last year. However, in [...] The relative lack of Chinese EVs on the road in North America and most of Europe has been a deliberate government policy choice, with most nations implementing tariffs to protect their domestic manufacturing base. Less than a year ago, the U.S. and Canada imposed 100% tariffs on imported Chinese EVs, while the E.U. imposed 17-35% tariffs on EV firms producing in China – Tesla received a lower 7.8% tariff from the E.U. on vehicles produced in China.
